text: Support Azure Service Bus as an alternative transport for the order saga in local dev, using its emulator.
Which queue broker should our laptops and the deployed environment share so the order workflow behaves identically in both places?
Saga won't start against the Service Bus emulator locally: creating subscriptions returns HTTP 500 and Wolverine's own queues never get created. Same code runs fine on Rabbit.
We run a dozen repos and every one of them re-learns the same hard-won engineering lessons. Propose how lessons get captured once and reach all of our repos.
Should every project ship its own keyword-activated helper agents, or should the whole company draw on one shared stock of past lessons that gets enforced everywhere?
Three teams hit the exact same timezone bug within a month. Another team had already fixed and documented it, but nobody's agent setup knew, because each repo only carries its own notes.
Implement a bulk 'send announcement' action in the admin API that emails 20,000 subscribers and records delivery status for each.
The PDF export button on the reports page takes about 40 seconds to respond and the browser just spins. How should I restructure the endpoint so users aren't left waiting?
Users get 504 Gateway Timeout when importing a big CSV via POST /imports; the data still ends up partly loaded and retries create duplicates.
Write the unit tests for the new RefundService: partial refunds, refunds after the 30-day window, and refunding an order that was already refunded. xUnit and NSubstitute.
Add coverage for the double-spend protection in the wallet transfer code: two simultaneous transfers from one balance, and a retried request carrying the same idempotency key.

Someone refactored the tenant-isolation check and the suite stayed green; reviewers couldn't tell what the five bare assertions in the old spec were supposed to guard, so the regression slipped through.
Domain code in our .NET solution keeps importing Infrastructure namespaces. Set something up so these layering violations get caught before merge.
Domain classes should never touch persistence namespaces. What's the lightest way to stop people breaking that layering as the codebase grows to a handful of aggregates?
Found a PR where a Domain entity uses an EF Core attribute and calls a repository class from Infrastructure. CI was green and nobody noticed until much later.
Add Application Insights telemetry to the AppHost for the catalog and orders services so they report to Azure Monitor once deployed.
Hook up our cloud monitoring service to the .NET distributed app host so each microservice reports telemetry in production, while developers still get a working F5 on their laptops.
After merging the telemetry PR nobody can run the solution on their machine: the dashboard shows 'Missing subscription configuration' and the API and worker containers never start.
Upgrade our Aspire AppHost to 9.4 and pick up the newer Redis hosting integration.
Bumping the version of our .NET local-orchestration host project and a couple of its integration libraries. What's the right way to do the upgrade so startup stays healthy?

After updating one of the Aspire hosting packages, the local app won't start: it exits saying a newer version of the AppHost package is required. On another branch it died with a type-load error at startup.
Add RabbitMQ and SQL Server containers to the Aspire AppHost and connect the Orders API and the worker to them.
Set up our local dev stack so the API and worker boot alongside Postgres and a broker, and come up cleanly on a cold machine with nothing cached.
On a fresh clone the API and worker exit within seconds with 'Connection refused' to the broker; rerunning a minute later works. Only the first run after pulling images fails.
Add GET /api/documents/{id} and DELETE /api/documents/{id} so users can fetch or remove their uploaded documents; each document belongs to one user account.
We're adding an endpoint for customers to download their invoice PDFs by invoice number. Invoices sit in a shared table. What do we need to confirm before shipping it?
A user told us that by changing the number in the URL he could see another customer's saved addresses. The build and unit tests were green and nobody noticed for months.
Order submission must check stock for each of up to 50 line items against the Inventory API before accepting the order. Implement that validation step and keep the endpoint snappy.
Our checkout loops through the cart and pings the pricing API once per item, and it crawls on big carts. How can I speed this up without hammering the other team's API?
Submitting an order with 40 lines takes 12 seconds, the Inventory team says we're flooding them with 40 simultaneous requests, and occasionally half the lines get reserved while the rest fail.
Nightly job: mark every subscription as expired when its end date is more than 30 days in the past. The table has about 2 million subscriptions; EF Core on Postgres.
Write a maintenance task that deactivates stale sessions older than a week and purges soft-deleted comments; both tables hold millions of entries.
The archive-old-orders job eats 6 GB of memory and runs 40 minutes before the container gets killed, though it's fine on staging with a few hundred orders.
Add an UpdateProductPrice command handler to the catalog service; product details are cached in Redis by ProductId and served to the storefront page.
Support wants to rename a store location from the admin panel and see the new name on the public site immediately; location data is kept in Redis for fast reads.
Customers still see the old price for up to 10 minutes after an admin changes it, and refreshing doesn't help, even though the database already has the new value.
Document in the integration test factory why we seed the catalog the way we do. The background is in STATUS.md right now.
While annotating the retry helper I want to point readers to where the design reasoning lives. Where should those pointers go so they stay valid over time?
Opened the test factory source and the note says 'see STATUS.md section 4 for why', but that section is gone and nobody knows the reason for the hack.
In the checkout handler, after saving a new order, call the shipping-rate partner API for a quote and publish an OrderPlaced event to the bus; store the quote on the order.
In the signup flow, once the user record is inserted, we have to hit the external fraud-scoring service and send a welcome message through RabbitMQ before returning.
Under load tests we get 'timeout expired obtaining a connection from the pool' errors on checkout, but the SQL is trivial and database CPU sits idle.
Add a monthly revenue-by-region report endpoint to the finance API using Postgres window functions and percentiles; the EF Core model already has the Orders and Regions tables.
I'd like to hand-write the SELECTs for a couple of new reporting screens because the LINQ for them is unreadable. How should I wire that in next to the existing EF Core DbContext?
In one request our new reporting helper can't see the order EF just saved, and after an exception that order isn't rolled back like everything else. Pool stats also show extra connections.
Add a GET /customers/{id}/orders endpoint returning open orders with line totals. I want the data access shaped so the logic is easy to unit test with fakes.
Building the invoicing feature in .NET with EF Core. What's the best way to shape the data access so the command classes can be exercised with stand-in fakes?
Our order-command unit tests with the stubbed store all pass, but in production the same LINQ filter throws a translation error. The in-memory list accepted it fine.
Switch order processing from synchronous HTTP calls to publishing events on the message broker. Implement the publisher, the consumer service and the topology changes.
We've just moved the inventory service behind a queue instead of calling it straight. Besides the implementation itself, what else should land alongside it in the pull request?
Review bot flagged a direct DB call from the API in my PR, but we removed that months ago. Our architecture picture still shows it and reviewers keep citing it.
Choose the messaging technology for order notifications between our services; the requirement is that nothing gets dropped when a subscriber is offline for an hour.
Our manager wants Kafka for the payment events because he heard queues can drop data. Each event only needs to be handled by one consumer once sent. Is that justified?
Using Redis pub/sub for invoice events: whenever the consumer restarts, everything published while it was down is gone and customers never get their emails.
Fix the repeated bug where handlers call SaveChanges inside a loop; the review turned up the same pattern in four places. Patch them all and open a PR.

Code review caught the third instance this quarter of someone forgetting cancellation tokens in async endpoints. We patched this one; what else should we do so the team isn't relying on reviewers spotting it?
Same antipattern, third time in two months: someone adds a blocking .Result call in a controller, we fix it in review, then a different dev reintroduces it a few weeks later.
Implement the CreateInvoice use case: it must reject duplicate invoice numbers and customers over their credit limit, and the API should give callers clear failure responses.
New feature for the booking service: return something sensible when a seat is already taken or a hold has expired, instead of the generic 500 we have today. How should those failures be modelled?
The same invalid-input case gives a 400 ProblemDetails from the orders API but a 200 with an error object from the new shipping API; clients are confused and controllers look inconsistent.
Spin up a prototype branch to try an LLM-based triage bot on our support queue: wire the model API, a small classifier and a Slack integration.
Starting a quick spike on semantic search for our knowledge base. What should be settled on day one so a throwaway trial doesn't turn into a permanently maintained service?
hey, remember the recommendation demo someone hacked together six months ago? It's now in our prod dependencies, has a pager rotation nobody agreed to, and no one recalls who asked for it.
Extend the CreateOrder use case with promo codes, loyalty point redemption and gift-wrap options; its command, validator and handler already all live in one C# file.
The handler for importing invoices has grown huge after recent additions, and a reviewer said it's painful to navigate. How do we tidy it while keeping the vertical-slice organisation?
Merge conflicts keep hitting RegisterUser.cs: it's now over 900 lines holding the command, validator, handler and DTOs, and nobody can review PR diffs on it any more.
Collapse Catalog.Application into Catalog.Api and delete the empty project folder; move the remaining classes over.
Reorganizing the repo: relocating shared helpers to a new folder and removing a retired module. What else could break besides what the compiler flags?
Docker build for the catalog image fails with 'COPY failed: file not found' pointing at a project folder we collapsed last quarter. CI never flagged it until the redeploy.
Remove the legacy RabbitMQ transport from the platform: delete the adapter classes, drop the config keys, and update the README sections that mention it.
We retired the old metrics counter and message transport last sprint. How do I make sure nothing in the repo still describes or references them?
Months after we removed the gRPC transport, a new teammate followed the architecture guide and got stuck, and the on-call dashboard still lists an alarm for a counter nothing increments.
Add a new Invoice aggregate with a Guid primary key, a factory method and an EF Core mapping to a clustered SQL Server table.
Inserts into our biggest SQL Server table keep slowing down as it passes 50 million rows, and index maintenance is heavy. The key column is a unique identifier generated on the client. Ideas?
Insert throughput on Orders keeps degrading and the clustered index is 95% fragmented a week after every rebuild. Page splits are everywhere in perf monitor.
Wire up bearer token validation in the orders API against our Keycloak realm. In docker-compose Keycloak is reached at an internal address without TLS; production uses the corporate identity host.
Set up sign-in integration for the new microservice so it trusts tokens issued by our identity server. Local environments use a container reachable on an unencrypted internal URL.
Security scan flagged that our staging API fetches its signing keys from an http:// authority URL, and neither startup nor the logs complained. How did this get through?
Add a consumer for the PaymentCaptured event in the loyalty service that adds points to the customer's balance, using RabbitMQ with an outbox on the publishing side.
Build a subscriber on our message bus that, when an order ships, decrements stock levels and emails the warehouse. Messages come from a durable queue and are acknowledged after processing.
Several customers received their welcome bonus twice and stock counts dropped too far after the broker restarted overnight. We never saw any failed messages in the dead-letter queue.
Create a Keycloak realm for the new payments app with an SPA client and an API client, and get it running in docker-compose for local dev, staging and prod.
The staging login server issues credentials that last an hour while production's expire after five minutes; how do we make all environments behave the same for sign-in sessions?
After upgrading Keycloak, access tokens suddenly last much longer and a refresh token can be reused, though nobody touched our settings. Behaviour also differs between staging and prod.
Add logging to the CSV import worker so ops can see what it did: which user triggered it, how many rows were imported, and which files failed. Serilog is already wired up.
Instrument the payment retry service with diagnostic output so we can search by customer and order in Seq, including inside the batch job that handles thousands of invoices at once.
Seq can't filter by UserId any more and the nightly sync log is 3 GB; we also get an ArgumentNullException from a log scope when anonymous requests come in.
The product search endpoint feels slow to the team, so make it faster. It's an EF Core LINQ query with a few Includes, hit roughly 200 times a minute.
Our report-generation handler seems sluggish, so I plan to rewrite its inner loops with pooled buffers and make every method return a lighter async type. Worth doing?
Latency on /search is exactly the same as before last sprint's speedup PR, yet memory is up 30% and the code is much harder to follow. Was any of it worth it?
Add a middleware that stamps each request's user ID and a request GUID into the logging scope, and register it in the shared ServiceDefaults pipeline setup used by all our APIs.
I want log entries for each API call to carry who made the call plus a per-request tracking identifier, including calls that get turned away at the door. Where in Program.cs does that hook go?
Logs for 401 and 403 responses show UserId empty, though successful requests carry it fine, so I can't tell who is hitting forbidden endpoints.
Rename the Customer.Phone column to MobileNumber and make it required. The column has been in production for a year and holds nulls for some customers; EF Core on Postgres.
The schema script that created our Product table lacks a maximum length on Name, and it already ran on staging and production. What's the right way to get that limit in?
Staging's database schema differs from dev although both run the same code version; dotnet ef database update says nothing is pending, yet a column is missing on staging.
Build an admin page listing all customers with their order count and last order date, using EF Core.
The team dashboard showing each project with its members and latest activity feels sluggish on real data though it was instant with my seed data. How should the data fetching be restructured?
Customers list endpoint takes 8 seconds in prod with 2,000 rows but is instant locally; SQL profiler shows thousands of nearly identical SELECT statements for one request.
Let several support agents edit the same customer ticket's notes and priority from the admin UI; add the update endpoint and form for ticket details.
Add a save button to the shared price-list screen on the tablet app, where multiple warehouse staff are editing the same product entries during the day.
A customer says the discount they set on Monday vanished; the audit trail shows another admin saved the same promo an hour later, and nobody got any error or warning.
Add GET /orders returning all orders for the logged-in tenant with an optional status filter, for the new reporting dashboard.
Build an API route that returns the complete invoice history for a customer so the mobile app can display it; some accounts have hundreds of thousands of invoices.
API pod got OOM-killed right after a partner hit /audit-events with no query params, and the admin UI's later pages take 30+ seconds to load on the big table.
Delegate to the agent: build the new multi-tenant authorization model for the API, including tenant resolution middleware, policy handlers and migrating all existing endpoints.
Planning to let Claude loose on a big refactor of our messaging transport overnight and read the pull request tomorrow morning. Good plan?
The agent's PR for the new bounded context came back at 4,000 lines, half its assumptions are wrong, and its design choices can't be untangled. We've lost three days.
Make our API's failure replies include a reference the user can quote to support, so we can find the matching request in the logs. Add it in the global exception middleware.
Customers contacting the helpdesk need a reference number for the problem they hit so we can look up what happened; wire that into the JSON body our 500s return.
Pen-test finding: the JSON body of our 500 replies contains a long 00-xxxx-xxxx-01 string plus the raw exception message and an entity GUID. Security wants to know why that is exposed.
Scale the checkout API to three replicas behind the load balancer. The /login endpoint allows only 5 attempts a minute per client IP and that has to keep holding.
We're bumping the auth service from one pod to four next sprint. Login should allow just 5 tries per minute per client, so what do I need to watch with the throttling setup?
After scaling to 4 pods, brute-force attempts on /login get through at roughly 20 a minute even though config says 5. No errors or warnings anywhere.
Orders: POST create-order endpoint for our CQRS service, with the input type for the body and the handler that persists it.
What should I call the type that carries data into a write operation in our CQRS service? Right now everything is suffixed identically and it's hard to tell inputs from outputs.
Onboarding feedback: nobody can tell from the type names in /Orders whether something goes through the write pipeline or is just a read shape. Everything looks the same.

New SendDigest flow in the notification service: take the incoming event, check that recipient and template are present, render the email and send it. Nothing gets saved to a database. How should I structure the types and projects?

I'm starting a small worker that converts incoming webhooks into SMS messages and stores nothing itself. Should I scaffold the usual layered setup with entities, factories and a separate domain library?
New hire complains that a throwaway request type, never saved anywhere, comes with a static factory, private setters and a status enum, and takes four files to understand. Is this intended?
Add a customer lookup box to the admin screen that finds accounts by typing an email address, regardless of upper or lower case. The accounts table has about 20 million rows.
Users should be able to look up a record by typing a username with any capitalization, and results must come back instantly even though the table is huge.
Searching users by email takes 8+ seconds in prod now that the table passed 10M rows, and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan even though email has an index.
Write integration tests for the RabbitMQ publisher; the test project needs a sample connection string and API key that the parser will accept.
Our CI gate for leaked passwords is failing on my branch because of a dummy token in the sample config for the unit suite. What's the cleanest way to deal with that?
Gitleaks job keeps failing on my PR even though I removed the offending string in the latest commit; the earlier commit still gets flagged and the build stays red.
Fix: the connection string from the environment variable is ignored in Production because appsettings.Production.json takes precedence. Make the change and wrap up the task.
Tracked down a nasty ordering quirk in middleware registration that contradicts the framework documentation. Patch is ready to commit; anything else I should do with this discovery besides merging?
Same weird timeout bug bit a second teammate this week. The fix was committed months ago, but the only explanation is buried in one commit message and he burned an afternoon rediscovering it.
Add a consumer for the order-placed queue in the Fulfillment service, using Wolverine and RabbitMQ, that reserves stock and then publishes a stock-reserved event.

Our payments consumer reads from a broker queue and must not drop an in-flight item if the process gets killed mid-handling. How should the subscribing side be configured in our .NET messaging library?
After a pod got OOM-killed, three orders that were being processed vanished: the broker shows them acked, but there's no handler result and no error. The sending side uses the transactional outbox.
Add a Wolverine middleware class with Before and Finally steps that start a stopwatch and log the handler duration for all message handlers in the orders service.
Need a hook that wraps each message consumer in our .NET service bus library and times it. The analyzer says my helper functions on that class don't use any object state.
App crashes on startup with InvalidWolverineMiddlewareException right after I registered my new timing class; it compiles fine and the unit tests pass.
Add the Wolverine Azure Service Bus transport to our messaging project so the Billing service can publish to topics.

Bringing our Wolverine messaging stack up to the newest minor this week. The automation bot already raised a combined update, but I'm also introducing a new transport extension in the version manifest. What should I check?
App builds fine but in staging the RabbitMQ listener throws MissingMethodException on a core Wolverine type at startup. Nothing changed in our code, only a version bump merged by the bot.
Add endpoints so a customer can view and cancel their own orders, returning 403 when they try someone else's order.
Users should only be able to read their own invoices. Where in the code should the 'is this logged-in person the owner' decision live?
Our order handler tests need a mocked web request carrying a fake logged-in user just to run, and we can't reuse the handler from the queue consumer because there is no request there.
Add the Bogus package to Catalog.Tests and Orders.Tests so we can generate fake customer data in the tests.
How do we stop our twenty-odd .NET apps in the solution from ending up on different releases of the same NuGet library, and make upgrading it a quick single edit?
Build output shows two services resolving different releases of Newtonsoft.Json and one throws MissingMethodException at runtime; nobody can tell which csproj bumped it.
Add a payment-failed compensation step to the order flow: if payment fails after stock is reserved, release the stock and mark the order cancelled.
Our order workflow is just a handful of event handlers reacting to each other. At what point should we bring in a central coordinator engine like a workflow service?
Support asked where order 4812 is stuck and nobody can say without grepping event logs across four services, and now the rollback steps need timeouts and an approval wait.
Prevent static mutable collections (static Dictionary or List fields) from being merged into any of our services; we've been bitten by concurrent access before.
We have a coding rule that's too context-dependent for any lint rule to check, so how do we make sure it's actually followed instead of just written in the wiki?
A static mutable dictionary got merged again and caused intermittent corruption under concurrent requests. Code review missed it and nothing in the pipeline complained.
Make the correlation ID, user ID and session ID appear in logs and traces for the consumer that processes OrderPlaced messages, not just the HTTP API.
When a request kicks off background work through a queue, how do we keep the tracking identifiers attached so one customer journey can be followed end to end in the logs?
In log search an order request's trace stops the moment it drops onto the queue; the consumer's log lines carry no correlation id or user at all.
Evaluate whether we should adopt Dapr for service-to-service calls, pub/sub and secrets across our five .NET services.
Our architect suggests running a helper process next to every service instance to handle messaging, secrets and service calls for us. Is that worth it for an all-.NET shop?
Since we piloted routing calls through a companion container, p99 latency on checkout rose, compile-time checking of our service contracts vanished, and messages sit waiting in a state table.
Ticketing: hold a concert seat for 10 minutes while the user pays and release it if they time out. Several API replicas run at the same time.
Two requests at the same moment shouldn't both be able to claim the last unit of stock across our several API instances. What's the simplest safe design?
Under load, two buyers both successfully reserved the same room for the same night, and duplicate order rows show up whenever the client retries.
Add sign-in to the storefront: customers log in with email and password and receive a token that the order and catalog services accept.
Where should accounts, passwords and session tokens for our backend services live: in our own user table and code, or somewhere else entirely?
Pentester forged an admin bearer token against our login endpoint by editing the algorithm field in its header, and three downstream services accepted it.
Add a read-through cache for product lookups: check in-process memory first, then Redis, then fall back to Postgres, and refresh it when a product is edited.
Product details are fetched constantly; we want a fast local layer sitting in front of a shared remote one before hitting the database, and updates must refresh both.
During a traffic spike the database gets hammered with identical queries whenever a popular key expires, and after an edit some pods still serve the old value for minutes.
Shorten the access token lifetime to 5 minutes and add a confidential client for the reporting service in `auth-realm.json` for Keycloak.
I edited the identity provider's JSON settings file to add a client and shorten token expiry; how do I get the local dev stack to use them?
Changed the token lifespan in the realm JSON and bounced the whole stack, but tokens still last 30 minutes and my new client gets invalid_client.
Upgrade the mocking and assertion packages in the unit test projects to the latest majors; legal flagged that one of them now needs a commercial subscription.
Legal says the package we use for expressive checks in our unit specs is now paid for commercial use. What do we move to without rewriting every spec?
Security flagged that our build now sends data to an external service whenever the mocking package is restored, and the build log shows a sponsorship message.
Get the integration test suite running on my new MacBook so I can work on the billing service locally; Docker Desktop is installed.
A new joiner on an Apple laptop can't get our container-backed specs to start locally, though the container engine app is open and healthy. How do I set up my machine?
DockerUnavailableException when I run the integration tests on my Mac, but `docker ps` works fine and Docker Desktop shows running.
Set up structured logging with scopes for the new .NET 8 worker service and make sure the log lines land in the same pipeline as our traces.
Should we pull in a third-party package for writing structured log lines with message templates and async sinks, or is what ships with the framework enough?
Our service logs go through a separate package's pipeline and never carry the trace id in the collector, while trace data does arrive. Sink config feels duplicated.
Kick off the architecture for a greenfield invoicing, payments and shipping product built by a team of four: propose the deployable units and database layout.
We're a small crew starting a fresh production app covering orders, billing and delivery. Should each area be separately deployed with its own data store?
Our five-person team split the app into five separately deployed services last year. Now every release is five deploys, simple features need network hops, and data drifts out of sync between them.
Add endpoints to the ASP.NET Core order service to list a customer's orders, fetch one by id, and create a new order.
Starting a new .NET web service for invoices; how should I define the routes so the business logic doesn't end up living in the HTTP layer?
Code review: our .NET API action classes have ballooned. Each action has validation, database queries and pricing rules inline, and we can't reuse any of it from the queue consumers.
Write a recovery background job that finds stuck orders, updates their status and publishes an OrderRecovered event, all atomically.
A scheduled sweeper running outside the normal message-processing path must save an updated row and announce the change to other components so both succeed or neither does.
Nightly job's order update rolled back after an exception, yet the inventory service still received the OrderRecovered message. Started happening after we upgraded.
Publish the OpenAPI document and a try-it-out docs page for the payments service so partner developers can browse every endpoint.
Make the auto-generated catalogue of all our routes, with its try-it-out playground, available to external integrators on the live site.
Pen test finding: requesting `/openapi/v1.json` on the production host returns every endpoint, schema and auth requirement with no login, and the docs page loads too.
Add distributed tracing and request metrics to the orders API so we can ship them to Datadog now and possibly Grafana Cloud later.
We want monitoring data from our services sent to whichever observability backend finance picks next quarter, without rewriting app code each time we switch.
Our tracing dashboard is flooded with thousands of tiny spans for /health every few seconds from the Kubernetes liveness checks, and real requests are hard to find.
Add `GET /products/search?q=` returning products whose name contains the query text, over the 5M-row catalog table.
Anything we should put in place ahead of launching a public typeahead lookup that examines every row of the catalogue table on each keystroke?
DB CPU pinned at 100% and the site timed out for everyone; the slow log shows a single IP hammering search with `LIKE '%term%'` queries thousands of times a minute.
Configure ASP.NET API versioning in Program.cs so existing clients calling `/orders` with no version in the path keep working once we add v2.
What should the server do when a client reaches an endpoint without saying which release of the interface it expects: pick the latest, or something else?
We deployed v2 with a renamed field and a pile of old integrations hitting `/orders` with no prefix broke overnight; nothing in the logs said they had been moved.
Handle the new InsufficientStockException in the API so clients get a 409 with a consistent error body.
Make failures from any endpoint come back in the same JSON shape and include something support staff can use to find the matching server log line.

anyone else seeing this? Frontend gets three different error shapes depending on the endpoint, one 500 returns an HTML page, and when a customer says 'something went wrong' we can't find their server logs
Write integration tests for the place-order path that saves the order and publishes an OrderPlaced event through the outbox.
We approved our save-then-notify order path after reading the configuration. How can we really know a database write error won't still send the notification?
Customers got an 'order confirmed' email for an order that doesn't exist in the database. Reviewers swore the outbox config was right and every unit test is green.
Add API documentation to the new .NET 9 service: generate the description document, give developers a page to try calls, and make it consumable by our Spectral lint job.
Which tool should give us browsable endpoint documentation in a brand-new .NET project, now that the old popular package is gone from the project template?
CI's Spectral step fails on the new service because it wants a YAML description at the docs route, but we only expose JSON there.
Wire up a typed HttpClient for the partner shipping-rates API in the checkout service, with timeouts, retries and a circuit breaker.
What's the right way to make our outbound web requests to other services survive flaky downstream calls: timeouts, backoff, and backing off completely when a dependency is down?
When the inventory service went down, our API threads piled up waiting on it for 100 seconds each, then everything hit it again at once the moment it recovered.
Write integration tests for the order repository, including optimistic concurrency on updates and the Redis-backed session store. Keep them fast enough for CI.
How should we verify our data-access layer end to end so we can trust its behaviour with Postgres and Redis, not just with stand-ins in a throwaway process?
Repository specs are all green in CI but in staging a concurrent update crashes with a Postgres concurrency-token error, and a migration emitted SQL our suite never exercised.
Implement the PlaceOrder command: reject malformed input, require positive quantities and a non-negative total, and refuse to cancel an order that has already shipped.
Reviewer says our order code verifies the same things in the request model, the entity constructor and the status-change methods, and wants only one kept. Which should survive?
A cancelled order got shipped by a back-office script even though the API rejects that transition; apparently the rule only lives in the request validator.
Before confirming an order, the order service must check the product exists and reserve stock in the inventory service. Wire up that call.
How should our basket component get an immediate yes-or-no from the stock component, versus announcing to the email and analytics components that an order was placed?
Placing an order takes 4+ seconds under load and sometimes times out; traces show a chain of JSON HTTP calls between our backend services, each parsing large payloads.
v2 of the orders API: changed response shape, and v1 clients must keep working untouched. Decide and implement how both are exposed and documented.
How should callers choose which generation of our web interface they're talking to when we roll out breaking changes next to the old behaviour?
Our CDN keeps returning v1 payloads to clients that asked for v2, and in the raw access logs I can't tell which version any request wanted.
Upgrade WolverineFx from 5.39.3 to 6.8.0 across all services and make sure every host still boots.
Move our messaging library's NuGet packages up a major version, then confirm each service still comes up.
After the package bump every service crashes on boot saying no assembly generator is registered. Nothing in our own code changed.
Bump Wolverine to its next major release; our handlers take an interface registered through a factory lambda plus a pooled `DbContext`.
anyone know how to prep for the messaging framework's next major release? our handlers inject an interface built by a lambda registration plus a pooled EF context

Host won't boot since the upgrade: exception says generated handler code would need to resolve a type from the container at runtime, which isn't allowed. Only handlers using the pooled `DbContext` hit it.
Add an audit-logging middleware to the Wolverine handler chain in Program.cs and register it next to the existing middleware.
I'm adding another step that wraps every message handler in our .NET services; where in the registration list should it sit relative to the others?
Since someone tidied Program.cs, every rejected bad request leaves a stray log scope behind, and handlers log empty correlation ids on their first line.
Choose the in-process command handling and message bus libraries for the new .NET order platform; legal wants us to avoid paid license dependencies.
